tip: 'en' stands in for 'of it/some', and French won't drop it the way English does: 'Tu en as assez' is literally 'do you have enough of it'.
'lui' means both 'to him' and 'to her' – one word covers either gender, and it parks in front of the verb: 'lui parle', never 'parle à lui'.
Counting forces an 'en': 'Tu en as combien' carries a 'of them' that English drops – 'how many do you have (of them)'.
In the passive, the participle agrees with the subject: 'construite' takes an -e because 'la maison' is feminine.
Reflexive verbs build the past with 'être', and the participle agrees with the subject: 'elle s'est habillée' picks up an -e for elle.
French 'resembles TO' someone: 'ressembler à'. So the pronoun is 'lui' (to him/her), not 'le': 'tu lui ressembles'.
'pour' marks a planned stretch of time, not time already spent: 'pour combien de temps' = for how long you'll be gone. Elapsed time takes 'pendant'.
'y' replaces 'à + thing': 'croire à' (believe in) collapses to 'y croire' – 'tu y crois' = do you believe in it.
'savoir' in the future often means 'find out', not just 'know': 'je saurai la réponse demain' = I'll learn the answer tomorrow.
French can't say 'want you to come' with an infinitive: 'vouloir que' forces the subjunctive – 'nous voulons que vous veniez'.
'aller' + infinitive is the everyday spoken future, like English 'going to': 'on va essayer' = we're going to try. Far more common in speech than 'on essaiera'.
A past participle never agrees with an indirect object: 'lui' sits before the verb, yet 'prêté' stays bare in 'je lui ai prêté ma voiture'.
'dont' bundles in the 'of whom/whose': 'l'auteur dont j'ai lu tous les livres' = the author of whom I've read all the books.
Doubt undercuts certainty, so French flips to the subjunctive: 'je doute qu'il vienne', not 'vient' – the same switch you get after 'ne pas penser que'.
To rewind and imagine a different past, pair 'si' + the had-form with a would-have clause: 'si j'avais su, je ne serais pas venu' = had I known, I wouldn't have come.
'devoir' in the conditional turns 'must' into gentle advice: 'tu devrais lire' = you should read, softer than 'tu dois' = you have to.
A superlative claim tips the que-clause into the subjunctive: 'la plus belle ville que j'aie jamais visitée' uses 'aie', not 'ai'.
In a positive command the pronoun hops behind the verb, joined by a hyphen: 'explique-lui' – but negate it and the pronoun jumps back in front: 'ne lui explique pas'.
Only -er verbs drop the -s in the 'tu' command. '-ir' verbs keep it: 'réfléchis', not 'réfléchi'.
For an unreal 'if', 'si' takes the imperfect and the result takes the conditional: 'si tu lui parlais... il comprendrait' – never 'si' + conditional.
Nothing slots between 'aller' and the infinitive – no 'à', no 'de', despite English 'going TO order': 'on va commander une pizza'.
The conditional softens a blunt wish: 'elle aimerait vivre' = she'd like to live, gentler than 'elle aime' or 'elle veut'.
'que' recycles the object into a connector: 'j'ai lu le livre' becomes 'le livre que j'ai lu' = the book (that) I read.
After 'que', the participle quietly agrees with the noun before it: 'reçu' stays bare for masculine 'le cadeau', but a feminine noun would force 'reçue'.
'Tu verras' = 'you'll see' is everyday reassurance, not a literal claim about eyesight: 'tu verras, tout ira bien'. Same use as 'on verra' = we'll see.
After 'si', French keeps the present even for a future 'if': 'si tu étudies... tu réussiras'. But 'quand' and 'dès que' DO take the future.
'arriver' builds its past with 'être', not 'avoir': the would-have form is 'serait arrivée', never 'aurait arrivé'.
'il aurait fallu' = 'we should have', but names nobody: 'falloir' only ever runs with a dummy 'il' – 'il aurait fallu réserver'.
English says 'when you finish', but French puts the future after 'quand': 'quand tu auras fini' = once you'll have finished.
English can drop the 'that' – 'the song you're singing' – but French can never drop 'que': 'la chanson que tu chantes'.
That 'ne' after 'craindre' isn't a negation: 'qu'elle ne mourût' means fearing she WOULD die, not that she wouldn't.
'fît' is bookish – the literary past subjunctive. Spoken French reaches for the present instead: 'il fallait que chacun fasse sa part'.
English says 'as soon as it has arrived', but French demands the future after 'dès que': 'dès que le colis sera arrivé'.
'quand bien même' = 'even if', but unlike 'si' it takes the conditional: 'quand bien même il aurait raison' = even if he were right.
'même si' = 'even if', yet it takes the plain imperfect, never the subjunctive: 'même si tu me suppliais'. (Contrast 'bien que', which does.)
Tucked inside a sentence, a question keeps normal word order – no inversion: 'où j'habitais', not 'où habitais-je': 'elle a voulu savoir où j'habitais'.
'faire' + infinitive = make someone do something, and the doer follows the pair: 'a fait travailler les élèves' – literally 'made work the students'.
In the passive the participle quietly agrees: 'peints' takes -s to match 'ces tableaux' – a match English has no way to show.
'je me suis fait voler' isn't 'I made someone steal' – 'se faire' + infinitive marks something done TO you: I had my phone stolen.
'il m'a été impossible' is literally 'it to-me was impossible' – that 'm'' names who couldn't do it: I couldn't reach her.
'conseiller' slips in a 'de' before the infinitive that English simply omits: 'conseillé de me reposer' = advised me to rest.
A reported yes/no question uses 'si' where a direct one used 'est-ce que': 'elle m'a demandé si j'avais faim' = she asked if I was hungry.
'se faire la malle' literally means 'pack your trunk' – slang for clearing off suddenly: 'il s'est fait la malle' = he ran off.
'insister' needs 'pour' before 'que', where English expects a plain 'that': 'insister pour que nous partions' – and 'partions' is subjunctive.
